name: Photo editors
summary: Where a photo editor loses the result: in an unnoticed change to a face, in processing a series, or in saving the file. And which jobs deserve a tool of their own.
lead:
A removed wire, a neatly cut-out piece of jewelry and a shot for print are each checked differently. A pretty preview inside the editor is not enough: a person needs a result they can examine, correct and use further on.

This breakdown follows the work with the image itself: control over the change, repeating it across several frames, and saving. That makes it easier to tell a useful narrow tool from one more set of similar filters.

audiencesArt.alt: Different jobs in the “Photo editors” category.

audiences.title: Lightly edit a portrait and still be yourself
audiences.body: For a light edit of a portrait, a person picks a specific change rather than a whole new appearance. Recognizable features, the strength of the effect and a comparison with the original are what matter to them. Some things about the shot they want to keep, even if the algorithm offers to remove them.

audiences.title: Prepare images for work
audiences.body: A working series needs repeatable settings, accurate product outlines and an easy way to carry on across devices. One good frame still has to be turned into a set of consistent images. What is valued here is predictable tools and saving that is easy to follow.

audiences.title: Make a personal shot or a keepsake gift
audiences.body: A family shot or a keepsake composite is prepared for a particular occasion and a particular recipient. The faces, the composition and its fitness for the chosen way of printing or posting are what matter. The original helps compare the result and go back to a different version of the editing.

sections.title: Change only what was intended
sections.intro: Automatic processing is useful as long as a person still recognizes the original and can control the result.

observations.title: Remove what does not belong and keep the rest
passages: One small, separate edit can change the whole shot: take out an unwanted object and leave the rest of the scene alone. The value of such a tool lies in the precision of the edge and in a clear way to check the result. For this job there is no need to master an all-purpose studio with dozens of modes.

Let people select the area they need, examine the place that changed and return to the original state. It is especially useful to test difficult details right next to what has to be kept. A specialized editor can stay one link in a toolkit if its result is easy to pass on without repeating an edit already made.

A wire against the sky and a wire over hair are cases of different difficulty. When testing the idea it is worth taking frames with edges, reflections and small details. A useful result includes being able to spot a bad edit and roll it back locally, keeping the other changes to the shot.

quotes.text: This app is amazing, especially the object removal feature. It's super easy to use and it makes the object disappear as if there's nothing there. I use this feature the most to edit some photos for friends, family, and myself.

Sure all apps let you down occasionally right? But this one has so rarely failed in my need to remove difficult items, jewelry, even nail art. Nail polish still perfectly intact. It's edge awareness is awesome!!!

placements.title: Remove what does not belong and keep the rest

observations.title: Keep the person recognizable
passages: “Improve the portrait” means different things: fix the light, remove a temporary detail, or try a pronounced styling. Automatically removing freckles, changing features and heavy smoothing can all go beyond the intent that was chosen. Recognizability here is judged by the person in the shot.

Separate the types of change from their intensity, and keep a quick comparison with the original. It helps to see an effect on its own before combining it with others. If the result is attractive but no longer looks like the person it should, being able to reject it matters more than one more automatically offered option.

A business headshot may call for an even background and even light, but not for a change of age or of the shape of the face. Separate settings help a person express that intent. A comparison with the original has to stay available after several steps too: only the user can decide whether the editing fits their job.

quotes.text: I LOVE how it doesn’t change me! It simply accentuates my best features and removes flaws that the i phone accentuates. For example, the wrinkles. The I phone camera lens ( the way it was designed with a curve, I think is what I read about)

I've been a dedicated user of all the YouCam apps for years now. I pay annually and screentime suggests I spend about 30% of my time using them on average every week. When they first integrated the new AI feature into the Pro Removal feature, I was horrified to find it was removing my freckles and moles automatically.

I just started using Citrus not too long ago. The only problem I have with Citrus is that it sometimes gets rid of details that I wanted to keep. On portraits it can make the skin look overdone if you leave it on its default setting.

observations.title: Repeat a style while allowing for each frame
passages: Grain, color and contrast can be a deliberate authorial choice. In one review a person returns to the same effect many times while preparing photographs for print. That is evidence of his own working method; his verdict on digital shots in general should not be taken as a rule.

Black and white treatment has a depth of its own: a ready-made color switch is often not enough. The author wants control over how the result looks. For a narrow editor that is a more substantial job than adding a few more similar presets.

At the same time, one style does not mean the same correction on every frame. An area that is too dark has to be fixed locally while the overall treatment stays. Across a series it helps to separate the saved base from the changes made to a particular shot; otherwise every repeat of the preset has to be corrected by hand.

quotes.text: I guess I've become something of a Daze Cam power user. I've used the app to process many thousands of photos to prepare them for printing. Digital photos of almost any era look terrible in print in their original form. I use Daze to apply a grain pattern that makes them look authentic.

I love this app! I take lots of color photographs that clearly lend themselves to black and white treatment, but many apps that will allow you to make the change don't have the number of options and effects to get a professional look.

I've had Afterlight forever, but it needs improvement. I use the filters less than other things but when I do, I'm reasonably satisfied. I use touch editing constantly because it's a relatively straightforward way to fix isolated too-dark or too-bright spots.

placements.title: Repeat a style while allowing for each frame

observations.title: Build a composition and leave it editable
passages: Compositing is interesting because you can build an unusual scene yourself: add a character, join family photographs together, or dress an image up for an occasion. The pleasure comes from your own decisions, so an editor needs to give precise control over the details, not only a set of finished templates.

A convenient path joins the overall view of the composition with work on a small fragment. Let people move elements, refine a cutout and go back to an earlier decision. A saved project is useful as a continuation of the thought: the finished image can be shown to family, and the composition corrected after what they say.

A finished collage and a saved project play different roles. The picture can be sent, but replacing one photograph a month later takes the layers, the fonts and the placement of the elements. So restoring a project is worth testing on a specific edit: open an old card, swap a shot and save the result again.

quotes.text: You can really get down to each individual pixel with this app; very intricate. I have used it for everything from superimposing characters to using it for ALL the weddings, events, & celebrations. I am continuously asked, 'How did you get that picture?'

placements.title: Build a composition and leave it editable

sections.title: Repeat a result that worked
sections.intro: For a series of shots, what matters is saved settings, individual edits and access to familiar tools.

observations.title: Process a batch without hidden exceptions
passages: When shooting products, background removal becomes repeatable work. An author who photographs jewelry values an accurate cutout on a phone. For that scenario it matters to keep a small detail of the product itself, not only to get a clean white background.

Across a series, a small difficulty repeats many times. Another author links a bad update to hours of lost work. A useful next step is to process a few difficult frames first, then spread the common settings across the rest and leave the individual exceptions to be fixed by hand.

The work can continue on a computer. A Lightroom user values the link between mobile files and the main catalog. So the handover has to preserve versions and changes that are easy to follow: a person has to know which frame has already been processed and where to pick up. That is a separate job from the speed of batch background removal.

quotes.text: I've used the app since the early days. It has consistently improved. I do jewelry photography. On the phone, Pixelcut is my go to for precise and reliable background removal when I can't get to Photoshop. Even PS Express is subpar.

I've used Photoroom for 3-4 years now. With every single update over that time it has consistently gotten worse. This last update is completely unworkable. I operate a jewelry resell business. Photoroom has cost me at least 8 hours this week alone in lost productivity.

This is a great app. It is useful for editing mobile images but also for editing Raw files. The full functionality and benefit of this app doesn't become apparent until you sync it with your desktop Lightroom catalog. This has been helpful.

placements.title: Process a batch without hidden exceptions

observations.title: Find a familiar edit after an update
passages: After an update a familiar edit can get harder for two reasons: the tool has moved, or it is no longer available. For a returning user those are different situations. Searching for the old command is pointless if the capabilities have changed, and relearning everything is excessive if only its place has changed.

Help people rebuild the familiar sequence of actions, and explain the substantial changes right next to it. New animations are no substitute for quick access to an edit used often. When testing a redesign, take the user’s old job and see whether he can carry it through to the same chosen result.

A returning user usually remembers the action: adjust a curve, cut out an object, apply a mask. A search across jobs like these and a short note on where the command moved help faster than a tour of all the new capabilities. This is especially clear in an editor used for work, where a familiar sequence is repeated many times.

quotes.text: The Snapseed app *was formerly* my favorite and most used photo editor. It *was* surprisingly sophisticated for how simple it was to make changes. It *was* approachable and also super easy to learn for new users. Navigation *was* intuitive.

Snapseed was the photo editor I recommended to everyone. It was clean, easy to use, and actually had really useful and powerful tools. Then came the redesign. What a godawful mess! They're so proud of their little animations when they show off the new design.

Update: Now pretty teeth feature is gone. guys please please tell your app developers to stop removing key features your members are used to!!!! Update: now the celebrity hairstyle hair transfer options are gone… why do you keep removing things?

observations.title: Understand the terms before a long edit
passages: Coming back to an app bought earlier, a person expects to finish a familiar job again. A new subscription screen may not explain what happened to the old purchase. In that case, restoring access, a changed set of features and the terms of a new service all have to be told apart.

In a review about collages the author lists the capabilities he paid for earlier one by one. This is not an argument about subscriptions in general: the person is trying to understand why his old way of working is now unavailable. The purchase history and access to saved projects are worth explaining right next to the offer of a new plan.

For a new user a similar problem shows up inside a trial edit. If every next tool requires an ad break, it is hard to hold a comparison of options together. One trial shot should travel the whole path to a file: then the terms are known before work on a large series begins.

quotes.text: I bought this app many years ago with a ONE TIME purchase and have been using it since. I have stayed loyal to this app and would have recommended it but today I went to use it again and was notified that I need to buy a subscription to download the app that I already own.

I first started using PicStitch in 2013. I paid for premium access to features way back when, only to open the app today to find these features (both originally free and what I paid for) all suddenly behind a paywall that's charging nearly $100/year.

The moment you open the app, it makes you watch an add, you watch an ad additionally so that you could attempt to adjust the picture, then if you want to go further and adjust another aspect of the picture, it's another ad, after you've done it again it's another ad.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Understand the terms before a long edit”.

sections.title: Get a file for the next step
sections.intro: Editing ends in a post, a print or a handover. Those requirements are worth knowing before the long work starts.

observations.title: Check the file outside the editor
passages: The image in the editor and the final file have to be judged separately. For a post, the size and the absence of unexpected elements matter; for print, the chosen format and how the details look at the required size. An effect that is pleasant on screen can turn out to be wrong for the next step.

Make a trial export part of the start of work on a series: show the settings, the watermark and the way things are saved. Keep the original, the editable version and a new copy distinct. When editing an old family shot it helps to compare the faces and the small details: added expressiveness is not the same as preserving the original content.

A separate expectation is to keep working on a photograph inside the familiar photo library, with the link to the original preserved. The author does not want to deal with new, unconnected copies. It has to be settled in advance what is being saved: a new picture, an editable project, or edits to the original. The check ends with reopening the file, not with a “done” message.

quotes.text: This app is great!! I wanted to print photos for a gift for my dad's 70th birthday. So I needed GREAT photos. I print photos using an app for a local store, and almost every photo gave me a 'low resolution' error. So I Googled how to fix that and found this app.

This app is very well featured and has a lot of controls and useful presets that can produce a very fine vintage look. However unfortunately it is also completely useless since the lack of control over output options means it only outputs a very low resolution image.

I would have paid the lifetime subscription fee in a heartbeat if this wasn't missing this vital feature: it does not operate as a Photos editing Extension. I don't want an app that creates NEW images that lose the original. Instead I want to edit my original in place.

placements.title: Check the file outside the editor

conclusion.title: The priority: a controllable edit and a usable file
conclusion.body:
The most substantial improvement here is to help a person finish a specific edit, notice a mistake and use the file further on. Object removal, portrait editing and a product series already have good tools. A new app has to win on a difficult stretch: a fine outline, keeping the features that matter, repeating settings, or carrying the work on to another device.

For a first test I would pick one such stretch and carry it from the source file through to reopening the result. The number of effects is secondary for now. The film look, monochrome and the headshot for work can all stay as modes of an existing editor; they call for a product of their own only if there is a noticeably better way to do their job.
